nominee.t: Confirmed Democratic nominee: won the May 19, 2026 Democratic primary with 286,612 votes (78.6%) over Will Boyd (9.7%), Yolanda Rochelle Flowers (5.0%), Jamel J. Brown (4.3%), Chad 'Chig' Martin (1.6%) and Nathan Mathis (0.8%); no runoff needed.

ballot.t: General-election ballot lists only Jones (D) and Tommy Tuberville (R) plus a write-in line; no independent or third-party candidate for governor appears in Politics1, the Alabama Reflector voter guide or Wikipedia's ballot table. Independents had until May 19, 2026 to file 42,458 signatures. The Secretary of State's certified candidate list itself was not retrieved.

oneliner.t: Democratic former U.S. senator (2018–2021) and former U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Alabama who prosecuted two Klansmen for the 1963 16th Street Baptist Church bombing, now the Democratic nominee for governor.

born.t: May 4, 1954, Fairfield, Alabama (Wikipedia; The Atlantic gives his age as 72 in July 2026, consistent)

hometown.t: Fairfield, Alabama (grew up there; Fairfield High School)

upbringing.t: Jones (legal name Gordon Douglas Jones) grew up in Fairfield, a steel town just west of Birmingham. His father, Gordon, worked at U.S. Steel and his mother, Gloria, was a homemaker; one grandfather was also a steelworker and the other a coal miner, and Jones worked in a steel mill while in school. He graduated from Fairfield High School, the University of Alabama (B.S. political science, 1976) and Samford University's Cumberland School of Law (J.D., 1979). He married Louise New in 1992; they have three children.

education.school: Cumberland School of Law, Samford University

career.role: Staff counsel, Senate Judiciary Committee (Sen. Howell Heflin)
U.S. Attorney, Northern District of Alabama (appointed by President Clinton)
Government relations and white-collar practice (worked from the D.C. office)
CNN commentator; Georgetown, Center for American Progress and University of Chicago fellowships; Biden administration 'sherpa' for Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson's confirmation (Jan.–Apr. 2022)

platform.t: One-year moratorium on data centers; no tax breaks for data-center companies; ban secret deals and nondisclosure agreements; public notice and impact studies.
Suspend the state gas tax when prices spike; fully eliminate the grocery tax; raise wages, including the minimum wage; end taxes on overtime; accountability at the Public Service Commission.
State earned income tax credit, more child care, free community college for adults without credentials, apprenticeship incentives, occupational-licensing changes.
Expand Medicaid; use the money to strengthen rural hospitals and mental-health and addiction services.
Ban elected officials from trading individual stocks; stronger state financial-disclosure rules; citizen ballot initiatives; expand early voting.
Put a state lottery before voters, with revenue going to voter-chosen priorities.
Opposes the CHOOSE Act education savings accounts: let current students finish but stop new applications.
Partner with localities on affordable housing; independent oversight and reform of the prisons, which his platform calls dangerous and unconstitutional.

promises.t: Impose a one-year moratorium on data centers.
Fully eliminate the state grocery tax.
Ban elected officials from trading individual stocks while in office.
Put a state lottery before voters.
Stop new CHOOSE Act applications and let current participants finish.
Create a state earned income tax credit and free community college for adults without credentials.

claims.claim: Expanding Medicaid would cover "more than 154,000 working Alabamians."

said.where: campaign Priorities page (item 4, as of access date)

record.t: Families USA (March 2026) estimates about 154,842 low-income adults could enroll under expansion after removing an estimated 36% who would lose coverage under new federal work-reporting rules. Alabama Arise cites 'up to 155,000.' The figure matches these advocacy estimates, but the source does not count how many are 'working'; it is the number expected to remain enrolled under work reporting.

claims.claim: Alabama is turning down "roughly $182 million in federal healthcare funding each year."

record.t: The number matches Families USA's estimate of $181.6 million for 2026, but that figure is state costs and lost savings (uncompensated care, existing Medicaid groups, mental health, inmate inpatient care) that federal expansion money could cover. It is not the total federal expansion funding forgone, which would be larger. The estimate comes from an advocacy group, drawing on PARCA's 2022 study.

claims.claim: "Data center developers are getting big tax breaks from Montgomery, and Tommy Tuberville is taking their money."

record.t: Alabama law has allowed data-center tax abatements of up to 30 years. A 2026 bill to cap them at 20 years passed the Legislature in April 2026; whether the governor signed it was not confirmed. Tuberville's state filings show a $25,000 contribution in August 2026 from Applied Digital Corp., a Dallas data-center developer tied to a proposed Brookwood project.

claims.claim: Tuberville called residents' concerns about electric bills, water use and harm to communities and the environment "bullcrap."

said.where: first TV ad (as described by ADN)

record.t: On July 13, 2026, Tuberville said of the claim that data centers will ruin the climate: 'bull crap.' In the same remarks he blamed opposition on Chinese social-media influence. The recorded remark was about the climate claim. It was not shown to be about electric bills or water, and on July 23 he said he understands why Alabamians might be hesitant.

claims.claim: Tuberville made more than 1,300 stock trades in the Senate, more than 250 involving AI or data-center companies (worth $5.2M–$14M), including 14 Alibaba trades.

record.t: The total fits Quiver Quantitative's count of 1,356 trades as of Oct. 2025. The AI/data-center subtotal and the Alibaba count could not be checked against Senate eFD (blocked). Disclosures give value ranges, so dollar totals are inherently imprecise. Jones did not allege any law was broken.

claims.claim: Tuberville is "wrong" on data centers (with his past remarks on gas prices).

record.t: Policy judgment. The gas-price remarks quoted in the ad could not be read (paywall).

claims.claim: "No one has ever — ever — questioned my being an Alabama resident for my entire life."

record.t: Records support Alabama residency: he and his wife have claimed a homestead exemption on their Mountain Brook home continuously since buying it in 2010. But after leaving the Senate he worked from ArentFox Schiff's Washington office, and more than 25 FEC receipts and a PAC record list that D.C. address. Lagniappe was questioning his records when he made the statement. He declined to share state tax receipts.

claims.claim: Data center developers are getting 'big tax breaks from Montgomery.'
claims.short: Data centers get big state tax breaks

said.where: first TV ad (30 seconds, broadcast and cable), as described by Alabama Daily News

record.t: Alabama's data-center tax abatements could run up to 30 years with no investment requirement. HB 399 (2026), which passed the Senate April 9, 2026 and went to the governor, caps them at 20 years (plus 10 more for qualifying local investment) and makes centers over 100MW pay some state taxes. Whether the governor signed it was not checked.

claims.claim: Tuberville is 'pushing to build AI data centers across Alabama.'

said.where: first TV ad (30 seconds, broadcast and cable), as described by Alabama Daily News

record.t: Tuberville is on record as a vocal supporter of data-center expansion in Alabama. But he attaches conditions: data centers must pay for their own power and infrastructure and not use fresh drinking water. His Oct. 6 ad also promises to end data-center tax breaks and let communities decide where they go. Supporting expansion is documented; the ad leaves out these conditions.

said.t: Said if Tuberville released his Alabama and federal income tax returns showing his home residence, 'I will do the same.'

did.t: Tuberville filed seven years of redacted Alabama returns on June 1, 2026 (federal returns not reported released). As of Aug. 10, 2026, Jones had not released his and did not respond to follow-up questions.

entries.t: 'The kids that are in there now, let them finish, but quit taking applications.'
Called the program 'ill-conceived' and vowed to 'stop the CHOOSE Act in its tracks', ending it or rolling back key parts before income limits lift in 2027.
Called for a six-month to one-year moratorium on permitting new data centers.
One-year moratorium on approvals of large data centers, an end to NDAs, and public input before deals.
Cited his work as senator pushing Alabama to expand Medicaid.
Proposes barring statewide officials from trading stocks and holding related investments for five years after leaving office.

votes.bill: S. 1, Strengthening America's Security in the Middle East Act of 2019
votes.what: Passed 77–23. The bill included security aid for Israel and provisions allowing state and local governments to penalize boycotts of Israel (BDS).

pac_note.t: Itemized PAC money reported by news outlets: two PACs (Speak Up PAC, Blue Hen Federal PAC) totaling $3,500 in December 2025 plus $1,000 from Sen. Duckworth's committee; 'just over $25,000' from PACs Dec. 2025–July 2026 (also IBEW PAC $5,000, United Steel Workers District 9 $5,000, Marengo County Democratic Executive Committee $3,000, GoDekalb PAC $2,500, Groundwork Project PAC $2,500, Democratic Majority Action $1,000); $21,200 in August; September $6,500 (Reflector) or $11,500 incl. Engineers Political Education Committee $5,000 (ADN). December 2025: more than 7,000 donors, more than 6,000 contributions under $100.

superpac_donors.pac: Highway 31 (2017 special election; spent 'more than $4 million' opposing Roy Moore)
donors: Senate Majority PAC ('predominantly funded by SMP')

money_history.office: U.S. Senate (Doug Jones for Senate Committee C00640623; candidate S0AL00156)

corp.t: Business and trade-group PAC money in his Senate career, e.g., American Institute of CPAs $10,000, Charter Communications $7,500, National Apartment Association $6,000, and Comcast/NBCUniversal and Lockton $5,000 each (2020 cycle). Other-committee receipts totaled $875,252 (2017–18) and $1,943,850 (2019–20), a mix of business, labor, party and ideological PACs. In 2017 the Highway 31 super PAC, 'predominantly funded' by Senate Majority PAC, spent more than $4 million against his opponent; SMP's own donors were not retrieved. No corporate contributions were reported in his 2026 state filings. His reported PAC money there is mostly labor, party and Democratic-politician PACs.

lobby.t: FEC-itemized pro-Israel PAC contributions in the 2019–20 cycle: NORPAC $5,150, JACPAC $5,000, Friends of Israel PAC $5,000, DMFI PAC $3,000, Pro-Israel America PAC $1,000 ($19,150 total). Track AIPAC has no entry for him, and 2017–18 pro-Israel PAC itemization could not be retrieved.

note.t: Not a current federal officeholder, so no current Senate disclosure. LegiStorm's index shows Senate disclosure filings 2017–2021 (candidate, annual and termination reports), each year with extension letters; contents were not reviewed. No Alabama Ethics Commission statement of economic interests was found. He had not released his tax returns as of Aug. 10, 2026. His stock-trading record as senator was not reviewed.

law_note.t: Jones's own farewell account: 'more than 25 bipartisan bills' passed and signed into law, including repeal of the military widow's tax and permanent HBCU funding. Sponsor-vs-cosponsor counts not verified (congress.gov/GovTrack blocked).

revolving.role: Government relations and white-collar practice (former senator)
revolving.t: Joined in May 2021 with former staffer Cissy Jackson and worked from the D.C. office. One ArentFox LDA registration checked (2022, Infectious Diseases Society of America) does not list him. A full LDA search for his name was not run.

democracy.t: After losing his own race, publicly congratulated President-elect Joe Biden ('my friend of over 40 years') and Vice President-elect Kamala Harris.

debates.note: Says his campaign accepted invitations from several organizations (number not stated) and challenged Tuberville to a series of five debates; no debate has been scheduled because Tuberville declined.

townhalls.period: July–Oct 2026 (documented: Dothan July 22, Huntsville ~July 29, Daphne Oct. 2; part of a 'statewide Town Hall Tour')

note.t: Born (1954) and raised in Fairfield, Alabama; educated at Alabama schools; career in Birmingham. He and his wife have claimed a homestead on their Mountain Brook home since 2010. After 2021 he worked from a Washington law office, which he says was remote work that did not change his residence.

checks.legal: CourtListener was blocked by this environment's proxy, so federal dockets were not searched directly. Searched news archives (AP, APR, Alabama Reflector, ADN, Lagniappe, Wikipedia) for criminal or civil cases, Senate Ethics complaints and bar discipline involving Jones. None found. Alacourt is paywalled and was not searched.
checks.foreign: FARA (efile.fara.gov) was blocked and not searched. Checked one ArentFox Schiff LDA registration and news; no foreign-government or foreign-business ties found. His Senate financial disclosures (2017–2021) were not reviewed.
checks.claims: Fixed sample: campaign Priorities page read directly (first 10 items are mostly promises; 2 checkable figures rated). The 'Meet Doug' bio page has no reachable URL, so bio claims came from his written statement to Lagniappe. Ads: his two most-covered 2026 TV ads (Sept. 9 data-center ad; Oct. 2 data-center/gas-prices ad) plus his Sept. 2 stock-trading claims. Ad spending is unknown. UPDATE 2026-10-08: Priorities page re-read; its items 1–3 and 5–8 are promises with no checkable figures. Added 2 checkable claims from the first TV ad (Sept. 9, 2026): tax breaks (true) and 'pushing to build' (partly). The second ad's (Oct. 2) script is behind ADN's paywall, so its specific claims could not be read.
checks.democracy: Not in the Senate for the Jan. 6, 2021 count (term ended Jan. 3, 2021). Searched news for his statements on the 2020 and 2024 results; found his Nov. 2020 congratulations to Biden. No statement on 2024 results found. Re-checked 2026-10-08: Wikipedia and The Atlantic (July 2026) contain no statement by Jones disputing 2020 or about 2024 results or Jan. 6. He was not a member of Congress at the Jan. 2017 or Jan. 2021 counts, so certification votes do not apply.

research_notes: NOMINEE/BALLOT: Nomination confirmed (May 19, 2026 primary, 78.6%). No independent or third-party governor candidate found in three listings; the Secretary of State's certified list was not retrieved. MONEY (state): fcpa.alabamavotes.gov was blocked by the proxy, so every gubernatorial figure comes from news reports of FCPA filings. Receipts ($5.87M raised since entering), disbursements ($3.7M) and COH ($2.18M) through Sept. 30, 2026 are from ADN (Oct. 6, 2026); the Reflector gives $1.12M raised, $1.5M spent and $2.2M COH for September. Monthly figures: Jun-26 is 'about $486,000' (Reflector); Aug-26 is '$1.1 million'. Outlets disagree on September PAC money ($6,500 Reflector vs. $11,500 ADN; ADN adds a $5,000 Engineers Political Education Committee gift). APR said he got no major donation in December, while ADN reported two unnamed $25,000 contributions; resolve on FCPA. No named top donors were reported, so top_donors is empty; it needs an FCPA pull. No outside spending in the 2026 race was found. MONEY (federal): FEC committee pages read directly for 2017–18 and 2019–20. ProPublica's 2018 PAC list failed to load, so 2017–18 pro-Israel and corporate PAC itemization is missing. Track AIPAC has no entry for former members, so no career pro-Israel total exists; the $19,150 is the sum of five itemized 2019–20 PAC gifts on ProPublica. The business vs. labor/ideological PAC split was not computed. Highway 31's $4M+ comes from NBC; SMP's donors and any Highway 31 FEC filing were not retrieved. DISCLOSURES: efdsearch.senate.gov was blocked. LegiStorm shows extension letters every year 2017–2021, so recordx.disclosure is 'extension'. missed_pct omitted (GovTrack unreachable). FEC RFAI/notices not checked (JS-rendered page), so recordx has only one of the two required items. No Alabama Ethics Commission SEI found. VOTES: 'na' per instructions, since his Senate service ended before the key-vote window. The Israel S.1 vote comes from the Jewish Virtual Library roll list, not senate.gov. CLAIMS: 7 claims, 6 checkable. The campaign site has no reachable bio page, so his widely repeated 16th Street bombing prosecutions are documented in the profile (PBS/AP, The Atlantic) but not entered as a campaign-page claim. EFFECTIVENESS: bills sponsored, enacted and CEL scores not retrieved (congress.gov/GovTrack/thelawmakers.org blocked). The 'more than 25 bills' figure is his own and unverified. OTHER: Lagniappe (Aug. 10, 2026) reports he has not met his conditional tax-return pledge. Note that Tuberville released Alabama returns but federal release was not reported, so whether Jones's stated condition was met is arguable. A 1988 defense of Tom Posey was used against him in 2017; that was legal representation, not a legal finding against him, so it is not recorded. No Israel-related public statements by Jones in 2023–2026 were found. Photo not added: the Wikimedia file name could not be retrieved. | 2026-10-08 claims pass: added 2 claims from his first TV ad: 'big tax breaks from Montgomery' (true, DCD on HB 399) and Tuberville 'pushing to build AI data centers across Alabama' (partly). Checkable-verdict claims now number 6. The second ad's script is paywalled at ADN. Checklist unchanged: democracy stays 'news' (no roll calls apply; statements via news); disclosures and ethics stay 'news' with no new items; the web-search budget was exhausted, and dougjones.com's 'Meet Doug' page has no reachable URL.
